title: Bash Redirection: The Field Manual
summary: A deep tour of how Bash wires up file descriptors — what redirection actually does to fd table entries, why redirection order changes meaning, how here-documents and process substitution feed data into commands, and how pipefail and PIPESTATUS make pipelines report real failures.

chapters.title: File Descriptors: The Foundation
points: A file descriptor is a small non-negative integer index into the process's per-process fd table; the kernel resolves it to an open file description.
Every process starts with three fds by convention: 0 = stdin, 1 = stdout, 2 = stderr.
Redirection never changes the program's code — it changes what fd 0/1/2 point at before exec runs the program.
Programs write to numbers, not to filenames: `printf` calls `write(1, ...)` and has no idea whether fd 1 is a terminal, a file, or a pipe.
Three-level model: fd number → open file description (offset + flags + status) → inode/file. Two fds can share one description.
The open file description holds the file offset, so two fds sharing a description share the write position — this is why `>&` duplication behaves differently than opening the same file twice.
Check a live process's table: `ls -l /proc/$$/fd` shows symlinks like `1 -> /dev/pts/0` or `1 -> /tmp/out.txt`.
Test if a descriptor is a terminal: `[ -t 1 ] && echo interactive` — the idiom behind tools that auto-disable color when piped.
`exec 3< file` opens a persistent fd 3 for the whole shell; `exec 3<&-` closes it. Bash allows fds 0-9 by name for user redirection.
`{fd}< file` (Bash 4.1+) lets the shell allocate a free descriptor into the variable `fd`, avoiding hardcoded number collisions.
Descriptors survive `fork` and, unless marked close-on-exec, survive `exec` too — that inheritance is the entire mechanism behind redirection and pipes.
Bash sets close-on-exec on descriptors it opens for its own bookkeeping, but NOT on fds you open with `exec 3<`, so children inherit fd 3.
Common mistake: thinking `>` is a shell builtin acting on a command. It is a syntactic operator processed before the command is even located.

chapters.title: The Basic Redirection Operators
points: `cmd > file` — truncate-or-create file, attach as fd 1. Equivalent to `open(file, O_WRONLY|O_CREAT|O_TRUNC, 0666)` then `dup2` onto 1.
`cmd >> file` — append mode, `O_APPEND`; each write atomically seeks to end, which makes concurrent appends from multiple processes safe for small writes.
`cmd < file` — open read-only and attach as fd 0. File must exist; no creation.
`cmd 2> file` — explicit fd number before the operator redirects stderr only; the digit must touch the operator with no space: `2>` not `2 >`.
`cmd n> file` generalizes: any fd number can be redirected, e.g. `3> trace.log`.
`cmd <> file` opens for both reading and writing without truncating — used for device files and read-modify-write on a fixed-size file.
`cmd &> file` and `cmd >& file` are Bash shorthand for `> file 2>&1`; `&>>` appends both. Not POSIX — use the long form in `sh` scripts.
`noclobber`: `set -o noclobber` makes `>` fail on an existing file; `>|` forces the overwrite anyway.
The file is opened by the shell before the command runs, so `> out.txt` truncates even if the command does not exist or immediately fails.
Redirections are performed left-to-right, after word expansion but before the command executes.
Redirections can appear anywhere in a simple command: `> out.txt echo hi` is identical to `echo hi > out.txt`.
`/dev/null` discards writes and reads as EOF; `cmd > /dev/null 2>&1` is the standard silence idiom.
Bash-only virtual paths: `> /dev/tcp/host/port` and `/dev/udp/...` open network sockets, and `/dev/fd/N` names an existing descriptor.
Gotcha: `cmd > file` with the same file as input, e.g. `sort file > file`, destroys the file — the shell truncates before `sort` reads a byte. Use `sponge` or a temp file.

chapters.title: Duplication and Ordering: Why 2>&1 Position Matters
points: `n>&m` duplicates: it makes fd n a copy of fd m, both pointing at the same open file description (a `dup2(m, n)` call).
Read `2>&1` as "make stderr go wherever stdout is pointing RIGHT NOW" — it copies the current target, it does not create a lasting alias.
`cmd > file 2>&1` — stdout is retargeted to file first, then stderr copies that target. Both land in file. Correct.
`cmd 2>&1 > file` — stderr copies the terminal (stdout's original target), THEN stdout moves to file. stderr stays on the terminal. Almost always a bug.
The mental model: redirections apply strictly left-to-right, mutating the fd table one step at a time.
Swap stdout and stderr with a temp descriptor: `cmd 3>&1 1>&2 2>&3 3>&-` — save 1 into 3, point 1 at stderr, point 2 at old stdout, close the scratch fd.
Send only stderr through a pipe: `cmd 2>&1 1>/dev/null | grep error` — reorder so stdout is discarded after stderr has been duplicated onto the pipe.
`n>&-` closes descriptor n; `n<&-` closes it for reading. A command writing to a closed fd gets EBADF, not silence.
`n<&m` is the input-side duplication, e.g. `read line <&3` reads from the fd opened earlier by `exec 3< file`.
`|&` is Bash shorthand for `2>&1 |` — pipe both streams into the next command.
Order matters against the pipe too: the pipe is set up before the command's own redirections are applied, which is why `2>&1` inside a pipeline sees the pipe as stdout's target.
Comparison row — `> f 2>&1` = both to file | `2>&1 > f` = stdout to file, stderr to terminal | `&> f` = both to file (Bash only).
Debugging trick: `exec 2> trace.log; set -x` sends the xtrace stream to a file; `BASH_XTRACEFD=5` redirects trace output to fd 5 without touching stderr.

chapters.title: Here-Documents and Here-Strings
points: `cmd <<EOF ... EOF` feeds the literal block to the command's stdin — Bash writes the body to a temp file (or pipe) and attaches it to fd 0.
Unquoted delimiter: the body undergoes parameter expansion, command substitution, and arithmetic expansion — `$HOME`, `$(date)`, backslash escapes all fire.
Quoted delimiter (`<<'EOF'` or `<<\EOF`): the body is completely literal, no expansion. Use this for scripts, AWK programs, and anything with `$`.
`<<-EOF` strips leading TAB characters (only tabs, never spaces) from body lines and the terminator, letting you indent a heredoc inside a function or loop.
The terminator must be on a line by itself with no trailing whitespace; a stray space is the number-one heredoc failure — Bash then reports `unexpected end of file`.
Here-string: `cmd <<< "text"` is a one-line heredoc; the word is expanded and a trailing newline is added.
`read -r a b <<< "$line"` is the idiomatic field split without a subshell — unlike `echo "$line" | read a b`, the variables survive.
Heredocs compose with other redirections: `cat <<EOF > out.txt` writes the block to a file; ordering of `<<` and `>` on the line does not matter since they hit different fds.

Multiple heredocs on one line are read in order: `diff <(cat <<A
1
A
) ...` — bodies queue after the command line, first delimiter first.
Heredoc on a non-fd-0 descriptor: `3<<EOF` attaches the block to fd 3 instead of stdin.
Common use: `ssh host 'bash -s' <<'EOF'` runs a whole script remotely with no quoting nightmare.
Trade-off: a heredoc is one blocking chunk of literal text — it cannot stream and cannot be regenerated; for dynamic data use a pipe or process substitution.
Gotcha: heredoc content is delivered on stdin, so a loop body reading `while read` from the same heredoc will consume the lines the outer loop needed.

chapters.title: Pipes: What a `|` Really Builds
points: `a | b` calls `pipe()` for a kernel buffer, forks both commands, dup2s the write end onto a's fd 1 and the read end onto b's fd 0, then closes the spare ends.
Both sides run concurrently, not sequentially — b starts consuming while a is still producing.
The pipe buffer is finite (64 KiB on Linux by default): a blocks on write when full, b blocks on read when empty. This backpressure is the flow control.
b exiting early closes the read end; a's next write raises SIGPIPE, which is why `yes | head -1` terminates instead of running forever.
Only stdout goes through the pipe by default; stderr still goes to the terminal unless you add `2>&1` or use `|&`.
Each pipeline stage runs in a subshell, so variable assignments inside the last stage are lost in Bash by default: `echo x | read v; echo $v` prints nothing.
`shopt -s lastpipe` (non-interactive, job control off) runs the final stage in the current shell so its variable assignments persist.
A pipeline's exit status is the status of the LAST command only — `false | true` reports 0.
`$PIPESTATUS` is an array of every stage's exit status: `cmd1 | cmd2; echo "${PIPESTATUS[@]}"` prints e.g. `1 0`.
Capture PIPESTATUS immediately — the very next command overwrites it. Copy with `status=("${PIPESTATUS[@]}")`.
`tee` splits a stream: `cmd | tee log.txt | grep err` writes to a file and continues down the pipeline; `tee /dev/tty` peeks at data mid-pipeline.
Comparison row — pipe: streaming, concurrent, no seek | temp file: buffered, sequential, seekable, needs cleanup.
Pipes are unnamed and anonymous; `mkfifo` creates a named pipe (FIFO) that exists in the filesystem and lets unrelated processes connect.

chapters.title: Process Substitution
points: `<(cmd)` runs cmd and substitutes a FILENAME that reads its output — on Linux, a path like `/dev/fd/63`.
`>(cmd)` substitutes a filename that, when written to, feeds cmd's stdin.
Mechanism: Bash creates a pipe (or FIFO), forks cmd attached to one end, and passes `/dev/fd/N` of the other end as an ordinary argument.
Solves the core problem that pipes only feed stdin: `diff <(sort a.txt) <(sort b.txt)` compares two live command outputs with zero temp files.
Avoid the subshell variable trap: `while read l; do n=$((n+1)); done < <(find . -type f)` keeps `n` in the current shell, unlike `find | while read`.
Note the mandatory space in `< <(...)` — `<<(` would be parsed as a here-document operator.
Multi-sink fanout: `cmd > >(gzip > out.gz) 2> >(logger)` sends each stream to a different consumer process.
`tee >(md5sum > sum.txt) >(wc -c > size.txt) > /dev/null` computes several things in one pass over the data.
Limitation: the substituted path is a pipe, so it is not seekable — a consumer that calls `lseek` or needs to re-read (some `sort -m`, `tar` on tape) will fail.
Limitation: the shell does not wait for `>(cmd)` to finish; the outer command can exit before the writer drains. Add an explicit `wait` or a sync point when the output matters.
The exit status of a process substitution is not reported in `$?` or PIPESTATUS — silent failure is the main hazard.
Not POSIX — it is a Bash/ksh/zsh feature; `sh script.sh` on dash gives `Syntax error: "(" unexpected`.
On systems without `/dev/fd`, Bash falls back to named FIFOs in `/tmp`, which changes cleanup and permission behavior.
Comparison row — pipe: one stream, into stdin | process substitution: many streams, as filename arguments | temp file: seekable, persistent, needs a trap to clean up.

chapters.title: Exit Status, `set -e`, and `pipefail`
points: `$?` holds the exit status of the last foreground command: 0 = success, 1-255 = failure; 128+N means killed by signal N (e.g. 143 = SIGTERM).
By default a pipeline returns only the last stage's status, so `curl bad-url | tar xz` reports success when curl fails and tar sees empty input.
`set -o pipefail` makes the pipeline return the rightmost NON-ZERO status, or zero if every stage succeeded.
`set -e` (errexit) aborts the script when a command fails — but it does not fire for commands in a condition context (`if`, `while`, `&&`, `||`, `!`).
`set -e` alone does not catch pipeline failures either; you need `set -eo pipefail` together.
`set -u` (nounset) errors on unset variables, catching the classic `rm -rf $DIR/` disaster when `DIR` is empty.
The standard strict header: `set -euo pipefail` plus `IFS=$'\n\t'`.
pipefail gotcha: `cmd | head -1` now fails, because head exits early and cmd dies of SIGPIPE (status 141). Wrap or filter that case explicitly.
`PIPESTATUS` gives per-stage detail that pipefail flattens; use it when you must know WHICH stage failed.
Local scoping: `set -o pipefail` inside a function stays in effect after return unless you save and restore, or use a subshell `( set -o pipefail; ... )`.
`trap 'echo failed at line $LINENO' ERR` reports where errexit fired; ERR traps are not inherited by functions unless `set -E`.
`cmd || true` deliberately swallows a failure under `set -e`; be explicit rather than accidental.
Comparison row — no flags: silent wrong results | `set -e`: stops on simple command failure | `+pipefail`: stops on any pipeline stage | `+PIPESTATUS`: tells you exactly which one.

chapters.title: Scope: Blocks, Loops, Functions, and `exec`
points: Redirect a whole compound block once: `{ cmd1; cmd2; } > out.txt` — far cheaper than opening the file per command.
`{ ... }` runs in the current shell; `( ... )` runs in a subshell — the parentheses form isolates variable and `cd` changes too.
Loop redirection applies to the whole loop: `while read l; do ...; done < input.txt` opens the file once and streams it.
Redirecting a function definition, `myfn() { ...; } > log`, attaches the redirection at every call site of that function.
`exec > log.txt 2>&1` with NO command permanently retargets the current shell's own stdout and stderr — everything after it is logged.
Save and restore around a permanent redirect: `exec 3>&1 > file; ...; exec 1>&3 3>&-`.
`exec cmd` WITH a command replaces the shell process entirely — same PID, no fork, no code after it ever runs.
Persistent read fd for interleaved reading: `exec 3< data.txt; read -u 3 line; exec 3<&-`.
The nested-read problem: a `ssh`/`ffmpeg` inside a `while read` loop eats the loop's stdin. Fix with `< /dev/null` on the inner command or `read -u 3` on a dedicated fd.
Log everything from inside a script while still seeing it: `exec > >(tee -a run.log) 2>&1`.
Subshells inherit the parent's fd table, so a redirection set before a subshell applies inside it.
`coproc` starts a background command with its stdin and stdout wired to the array `COPROC[0]`/`COPROC[1]` for two-way conversation.
Trade-off: block redirection is efficient but coarse — one failing command inside `{ }` still writes to the same log, so per-stage tagging needs separate redirects.

chapters.title: Common Mistakes and Their Fixes
points: `2>&1 > file` when you meant `> file 2>&1` — stderr never reaches the file. Remember: duplication copies the CURRENT target.
`sort file > file` truncates the input before reading. Fix: `sort file > tmp && mv tmp file`, or `sort -o file file` for tools that support it.
`cmd > file 2> file` opens the file twice with independent offsets; the two streams overwrite each other. Always use `2>&1` to share one description.
`echo x | read var` loses the value — the pipeline stage is a subshell. Fix: `read var <<< "x"` or process substitution.
Space between fd and operator: `2 > file` redirects stdout and passes literal `2` as an argument.
Trailing whitespace after a heredoc terminator causes `unexpected end of file`. Terminator must be alone on its line.
Using `<<-` with space indentation does nothing — only leading TABs are stripped.
Unquoted heredoc delimiter mangles bodies containing `$var` or backticks; quote it as `<<'EOF'` for literal content.
Redirecting inside `sudo`: `sudo echo x > /root/f` fails because the shell (as you) opens the file. Fix: `echo x | sudo tee /root/f`.
Assuming a pipeline succeeded because `$?` is 0 — enable `pipefail` or read `PIPESTATUS`.
Reading `PIPESTATUS` after any intervening command returns that command's status instead. Copy it on the very next line.
Forgetting to close `exec 3<` descriptors leaks fds; long-running loops can hit `EMFILE: too many open files`.
Expecting `>(cmd)` output to be complete when the script exits — the writer may still be running. Add `wait`.
Word-splitting a filename: `> $f` breaks on spaces. Quote it: `> "$f"`.
`cmd &> file` in a `#!/bin/sh` script is not portable; write `> file 2>&1`.

chapters.title: Recap: The Redirection Cheat Sheet
points: Model to keep: fd number → open file description → file. Redirection rewires the arrow at the first hop only.
Everything happens before the command runs, strictly left to right — that single rule explains `2>&1 > file`.
`> f` truncate | `>> f` append | `< f` read | `<> f` read-write | `>| f` force past noclobber.
`2> f` stderr only | `> f 2>&1` both | `&> f` both (Bash) | `2>&1 1>/dev/null |` stderr only down the pipe.
`n>&m` duplicate, `n>&-` close, `{v}< f` auto-allocate a descriptor into `$v`.
`<<EOF` expands, `<<'EOF'` is literal, `<<-EOF` strips leading tabs, `<<< "str"` is a one-liner.
`<(cmd)` = a filename you can read from | `>(cmd)` = a filename you can write into | neither is seekable.
Pipes stream concurrently with backpressure; SIGPIPE ends the producer when the consumer quits.
Pipeline status = last stage, unless `set -o pipefail`; `PIPESTATUS` names the guilty stage.
Script header worth memorizing: `set -euo pipefail` — and know that `| head` will now trip it.
`exec` without a command retargets the shell itself; with a command it replaces the shell.
Block form `{ ...; } > log` beats per-line redirection for both speed and clarity.
Decision guide: one stream into stdin → pipe; several streams as arguments → process substitution; literal text → heredoc; must seek or persist → temp file.
Verify anything with `ls -l /proc/$$/fd` and `strace -e trace=dup2,open,pipe`; `bash -x` shows the expansions, not the redirections.
